SOURCE: "AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents", Xiao Liu, Hao Yu, Hanchen Zhang et al. (Tsinghua, OSU, UC Berkeley). ICLR 2024. Extracted file is arXiv 2308.03688v3, dated 4 Oct 2025. This version adds claude-3 (opus) and glm-4, both scored after the task weights were fixed.

COVERAGE: 58 of 58 pages, all 177,248 chars. I read pages 1–9 and 17–58 in full, including appendices A–J (framework, per-environment grading, failure analysis). I skimmed the references (pp. 10–16) only for origins. Text extraction was clean.

CLAIMS
- claim: The best API models do far better than open models of 70B or less on the weighted overall score.
  number: API average 2.32 vs OSS average 0.51; gpt-4 4.01; best OSS codellama-34b 0.96
  setup: 29 LLMs, 8 environments, test split, CoT prompting, temperature 0, one run each. Only OSS models of 70B or less were tested.
  quote: "Generally, most OSS LLMs perform far poorer than API-based LLMs in AGENTBENCH(Avg. 0.51 v.s. 2.32). The most capable OSS LLM ≤ 70B within the evaluation scope rounds out to be codellama-34b, achieving an overall score of 0.96"
  where: p.8
- claim: The most common way to fail is running out of turns (Task Limit Exceeded), not breaking the format or picking a bad action.
  number: TLE share averaged across all models: OS 23.9, DB 8.0, KG 67.9, DCG 0.0, LTP 82.5, HH 22.1, WS 27.8, WB 35.0 (%). Invalid Format: DB 53.3, DCG 38.5, WS 17.2. Invalid Action: HH 64.1, DCG 10.2, WB 8.4. CLE is 3.5% at most.
  setup: Table 4, outcome shares for each environment averaged over all models
  quote: "The predominant failure cause in AGENTBENCHtasks isTask Limit Exceeded, revealing weak reasoning and decision-making abilities in LLMs."
  where: p.8 (Table 4 and §4.3)
- claim: Open models produce more format and action errors than API models, and they complete fewer tasks.
  number: Completed 61.5% vs 39.1%; IF 6.0% vs 10.4%; IA 4.6% vs 13.6%; TLE 24.9% vs 36.9%; CLE 3.0% vs 0.0%
  setup: Table 6, outcome distribution pooled by model type over all environments
  quote: "10.4% of the Open-Sourced model outcomes were marked as Invalid Format, in comparison to the 6.0% from Commercial API-based models. Similarly, Invalid Actions were seen more in Open-Sourced models (13.6%) than in Commercial API-based models (4.6%)."
  where: p.46
- claim: Most runs that hit the turn limit are stuck in a loop repeating themselves.
  number: >90% of TLE trajectories contain two responses with Rouge-L of at least 0.8 within the last 10 rounds. TLE trajectories average 25.5 rounds.
  setup: TLE trajectories truncated to their longest prefix under 3500 tokens. The repeat metric is P(n,t).
  quote: "more than 90% of the trajectories experiencing Task Limit Exceeded (TLE) demonstrate a significant level of repetition... at least two responses within the last 10 rounds sharing a Rouge-L score of 0.8 or higher"; "the TLE results contain a trajectory with 25.5 rounds on average"
  where: p.55
- claim: Completed runs are short.
  number: median 6 rounds, mean 7.95; median 1850 tokens, mean 2220.1
  setup: all completed trajectories
  quote: "the rounds distribution indicates a median of 6.0 and an average of 7.95, with the medium 50% of tasks ranging from 4.0 to 9.0"
  where: p.54
- claim: gpt-4 is best on 6 of the 8 environments and reaches 78% success on House-Holding.
  number: 78% HH SR; OA 4.01
  setup: ALFWorld, 1-shot ReAct-style prompting, gpt-4-0613
  quote: "gpt-4 presents the best performance on 6 out of 8 datasets in AGENTBENCH; on House Holding, it achieves a success rate of 78%"
  where: p.7
- claim: Every API model scores above 1.00 overall.
  number: >1.00
  setup: Table 3
  quote: "All API-based LLMs have an AGENTBENCHoverall score above 1.00."
  where: p.7
- claim: Code tuning helps on procedural tasks and hurts on strategic ones. Training on high-quality alignment data helps.
  number: none in the prose. Per-environment comparisons are in Table 3, e.g. WS codellama-34b 52.1 vs llama-2-70b 5.6.
  setup: codellama vs llama-2 on WS, DCG and OS; vicuna-13b vs llama-2-13b, which share a base model
  quote: none quoted for a number
  where: p.8, App. J.2.5 p.56
- claim: llama-2-13b and llama-2-70b score about the same, and the result held when the authors re-ran it.
  number: OA 0.77 vs 0.78
  setup: Table 3
  quote: "we were surprised to find that llama-2-13b and llama-2-70b perform similarly despite the significant gap between their sizes. After carefully checking and re-running experiments, the results are unchanged."
  where: p.8

How each environment is graded:
- OS: state or execution check. The task runs in a Docker container with init and start scripts. The checking pipeline is a chain of scripts: "The result is correct if and only if all the scripts exit with code0." In operation tasks the checker inspects system state, and the agent does not have to answer. 144 test samples, 8-round limit "by default". (pp.21–22)
- DB: state check for writes. Each sample's answer is "the hash code of the correctly modified table" for insert or update, and an exact answer-set match for select, ignoring order and normalising numbers. SR is a macro average over the three operation types. Runs in a MySQL Docker container. (pp.24–25)
- KG: answer-set F1 against gold entities (Freebase via Virtuoso). The authors also report exact match on the answer set and "Executability". The prompt allows at most 15 actions. (p.27)
- DCG: reward = 0.7×win rate + 0.3×damage rate against a scripted opponent. The agent gets five tries to produce legal format, then loses. (p.30)
- LTP: an LLM judge. gpt-3.5-turbo acts as host and checks which key points the agent hit (Game Progress). The authors admit the automatic judge "sometimes more tolerate for the agent", especially for OSS models. (p.35)
- HH: the ALFWorld simulator reports whether the goal is complete, giving SR. Invalid output is BLEU-mapped to the closest valid action. Three identical outputs in a row count as a failure. (p.39)
- WS: WebShop attribute, option and price matching reward on the purchased item, range 0–1. (p.40)
- WB: Mind2Web Step Success Rate, which compares each step with the reference action. This is a trajectory match, not an outcome. Each step is framed as multiple choice over top-10 candidates chosen by a small LM. Task SR was dropped because "even the best LLMs now can only achieve single-digit task success percentages." (p.43)

How the overall score is built: each task is rescaled so its mean across all evaluated models equals 1, then the rescaled scores are averaged. The reciprocal means become fixed weights for future scoring. Quote: "we produce the overall score by first resizing each task's average score to 1 across all the models we evaluate and then averaging the scores across all tasks for each model" (p.7). Weight⁻¹ (mean score): OS 10.8, DB 13.0, KG 13.9, DCG 12.0, LTP 3.5, HH 13.0, WS 30.7, WB 11.6 (Table 2, p.6). The stated reason is that a plain average "is heavily impacted by tasks that generally yield higher scores (e.g., Web Shopping".

Harness hygiene: each environment runs in its own Docker container and isolated task worker. Model, task and client servers talk over HTTP. Evaluation can resume after an interruption, and work is scheduled with Edmonds–Karp max-flow (pp.6, 20). Decoding: "we set temperature=0 (i.e., greedy decoding) in the inference on all tasks" (p.7). History is truncated to 3500 tokens, with an inserted "[NOTICE] 2r messages are omitted." (p.6). Splits: Dev 269 and Test 1,014 samples, about 11k inference calls for the test split (p.6).

LIMITS:
- Each model was run once, greedily, with no variance, no confidence intervals and no repeats. The authors reason that "Without multiple trials, repeated generations" CoT is the cheapest way to deploy agents. Nothing in the paper speaks to non-determinism.
- Only plain CoT/ReAct was tested, not reflection or search. OSS models were limited to 70B or less.
- The overall-score weights depend on the original model pool. claude-3 and glm-4 were scored after the weights were fixed.
- Two environments do not grade outcomes. WB is step-level matching against a reference path, and LTP uses an LLM judge that the authors call lenient.
- The HH BLEU fallback and the DCG five retries soften Invalid Format, so IF rates are not comparable across environments.
- The DB data was augmented with gpt-3.5-turbo. A bias check re-annotated a small batch with Claude-2 and tested only two models (Table 5, p.26).
- The model list is dated (text-davinci, claude v1.3). CLE occurs only for 2,048-context models.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al., 2023b) prompt format; CoT (Wei et al., 2022b); ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020b) and TextWorld (Côté et al., 2019); WebShop (Yao et al., 2022); Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023); KBQA as tool learning (Anonymous, 2023; Gu et al., 2023), Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008), GrailQA (Gu et al., 2021); functional-correctness evaluation from HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021); Docker (Merkel et al., 2014). The DB data reuses WikiSQL (Zhong et al., 2017), WikiTableQuestions (Pasupat & Liang, 2015), SQA (Iyyer et al., 2017), HybridQA (Chen et al., 2020) and FeTaQA (Nan et al., 2021). The paper names InterCode (Yang et al., 2023) as concurrent work.

CODE:
- DCG reward, p.30: `reward= 0.7×metric winrate + 0.3×metric damagerate`
- Repetition metric, p.55: `P(n, t) = #{(r1..rm)∈T | ∃i,j (m−n < i < j ≤ m ∧ RougeL(ri, rj) ≥ t)} / #T`
- OS checker rule, p.22: `ok = fk(o0, o1, ..., ok−1)`; correct only if every script exits 0.

FIGURES:
- Recommended: Table 4, p.8, "Portions of different types of execution outcomes in 8 tasks averaged across all models." One grid shows that failure modes depend on the environment: Invalid Format dominates DB, Invalid Action dominates HH, TLE dominates KG and LTP. That makes the case for logging finish reasons per environment faster than prose can. figures.py did not list it because it is a table.
- Alternative: Figure 9, p.55, "P(n, t), percentage among all TLE trajectories that there exists a pair of responses whose Rouge-L score is not less than t in the last n rounds". It shows that turn-limit failures are mostly loops.
- Figure 6, p.47, has an outcome pie chart for each model. It is busy.

PROBLEMS:
- Sample counts disagree within the paper. Table 2 gives KG test as 150 and WS test as 200, but App. D and H say "first 500 tasks/entries". HH uses "134 solvable problems" against Table 2's 50.
- The text says solving rounds "range from 5 to 50", but Table 2's largest value is 35.
- The Figure 6 caption says "Text Limit Exceeded" and J.2.4 says "Time Limit Exceeded"; both mean Task Limit Exceeded.
- Table 6's API CLE of 3.0% comes only from the text-davinci models.
- The bar values in Figure 1 (p.1) extracted without a caption pairing. I quoted the averages from the p.8 prose instead.
- The text contains no embedded instructions.
